description: Width tiers for Health and Physical Education, Years 3-4, ACARA v9. Covers all 19 standards across both Movement and Personal, Social and Community Health strands.
subject: Health and Physical Education

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor that meets the descriptor's command term. For capability standards (all HPE standards at Y3-4), this means engaging with the skill or understanding in at least one context sufficient to demonstrate the command term (e.g. 'refine', 'apply', 'describe', 'investigate'). Minimum is not 'easy' — it is the non-negotiable floor.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended, grounded in the most common elaboration cases. A class that has engaged with the standard thoroughly would reach this level — covering the main contexts, phenomena and skill applications identified in the elaborations.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add contexts, perspectives or transfer tasks — not harder versions of the same task. First Nations Australian directions are included as a default where elaborations indicate them; they are not optional enrichment but part of ACARA's intended scope. Sustainability, cultural comparison and community contexts appear frequently across both strands.
width_notes.elaborations: Elaborations are used as the primary source for typical_width and wider directions. They are treated as examples of the descriptor's intended scope, not a required checklist. Some elaborations describe the same activity at different specificity and are merged. First Nations elaborations are always represented in wider.

AC9HP4M01.minimum_width: Perform activities that combine locomotor and object control skills in at least one movement task or challenge; perform fundamental movement skills demonstrating weight transference in at least one activity; perform a basic movement sequence connecting jump, landing and balance.
AC9HP4M01.typical_width: Refine and apply fundamental movement skills across multiple new situations — combining locomotor and object control skills, exploring propelling techniques towards varied targets, demonstrating weight transference across different physical activities, coordinating swimming strokes, and performing sequences incorporating jumping, landing and balancing with controlled transitions.
wider: Design and perform original movement sequences incorporating multiple skill combinations, with deliberate use of movement vocabulary (weight transference, timing, body shape).

Explore how fundamental movement skill combinations are used across culturally diverse movement forms — including traditional First Nations Australian physical activities — comparing technique and purpose.
Investigate how weight transference and propulsion principles apply in water-based and land-based contexts, comparing the coordination demands.

AC9HP4M02.minimum_width: Plan and perform a simple movement strategy in one minor or small-sided game type and reflect on the outcome; perform a balance activity and explain how centre of gravity influences stability.
AC9HP4M02.typical_width: Apply and adapt movement strategies across invasion, target, net/court and striking/fielding game types; manipulate centre of gravity to enhance stability and explain the relationship between centre of gravity and base of support; evaluate an adapted game tactic using set criteria.
wider: Design a game rule or constraint that forces a particular movement strategy, trial it with peers, and analyse the effect on game play.
Investigate how movement strategy principles from one game category (e.g. invasion) are adapted for a fundamentally different game type (e.g. target), identifying what transfers and what must change.

Explore how centre of gravity and stability principles are applied in martial arts, gymnastics or traditional movement practices — including First Nations Australian activities — and demonstrate one application.

AC9HP4M03.minimum_width: Demonstrate at least two movement concepts (from effort, space, time, objects, people) in a movement sequence or minor game; describe the spatial or effort choices made.
AC9HP4M03.typical_width: Demonstrate all five movement concept categories (effort, space, time, objects, people) applied across minor games, rhythmic/expressive activities and movement sequences; use the body to demonstrate body shapes, symmetry and angles; manipulate space in game contexts to affect scoring and possession outcomes.
wider: Analyse game play (observed or participated in) to map how effort, space and people concepts interact — documenting movement pathways and strategic decisions.

Explore how movement concepts apply in expressive forms such as dance or martial arts from different cultural traditions, including First Nations Australian movement, comparing how each culture uses concepts like levels, pathways and timing.
Create a movement concept glossary with personal demonstrations and peer examples, connecting movement vocabulary to mathematical concepts (symmetry, angles, geometry).

AC9HP4M04.minimum_width: Participate in at least one physical activity and describe how the body feels before and during; explain what warming up does for the body; describe at least two health benefits of regular physical activity including one beyond physical fitness.
AC9HP4M04.typical_width: Participate in a range of physical activities at varied intensities; systematically notice and describe body responses across activity types; perform warm-up and cool-down routines with purpose explanations; describe how regular physical activity benefits sleep, concentration and overall wellbeing.
wider: Investigate and compare the body's response across activities of very different intensities (gentle stretching, sustained aerobic activity, high-intensity interval activity) and connect the responses to health systems (cardiovascular, muscular, nervous).
Explore how warm-up practices differ across sporting codes and traditional physical practices — including First Nations Australian movement preparations — examining why the differences exist.

Research how physical activity benefits documented in the Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines translate to daily life for children — including sleep, concentration and mood — using school-based examples.

AC9HP4M05.minimum_width: Participate in at least one physical activity in a natural or outdoor setting; identify at least two enjoyable aspects and at least one factor that might influence someone else's participation.
AC9HP4M05.typical_width: Participate in physical activities across different natural and outdoor settings; reflect on enjoyment factors and participation barriers; explore home-based activity using everyday items; examine how physical activity connects people to their community.
wider: Explore First Nations Australians' connection to special places and how these places are linked to physical activities — engaging respectfully with community knowledge and investigating what is unique about place-based physical culture.
Design a community physical activity event or plan that encourages participation by addressing specific barriers (e.g. cost, transport, equipment, cultural comfort) for different community groups.
Compare outdoor physical activity access and participation in urban, regional and remote Australian contexts, discussing how geography, infrastructure and community shape participation opportunities.

AC9HP4M06.minimum_width: Identify the key physical activity and screen time recommendations in the Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines; propose at least two strategies to increase their own physical activity or reduce sedentary time.
AC9HP4M06.typical_width: Explore the full Australian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines (activity, sedentary and sleep components); examine benefits of regular activity for sleep, concentration and wellbeing; propose and evaluate realistic strategies to meet recommendations across school, home and community contexts.
wider: Develop and trial a one-week 'active plan' tracking personal activity against recommendations, reflecting on what worked, what was difficult, and what would change.
Design an activity plan for a peer or community member who faces a specific barrier to meeting the guidelines — explaining how the plan addresses the barrier.
Compare the 24-Hour Movement Guidelines for different age groups and life contexts, examining why recommendations change and discussing what evidence underpins each recommendation.

AC9HP4M07.minimum_width: Apply at least one movement skill from a familiar context to solve a movement challenge in a new context; work with others to generate and trial a solution to one movement problem.
AC9HP4M07.typical_width: Transfer and apply movement skills across varied contexts (field, court, outdoor, gymnastics) to solve movement challenges; draw on prior knowledge in outdoor activity settings; collaboratively design and trial solutions across partner, group and team movement challenges.
wider: Lead a structured problem-solving cycle for a complex movement challenge (plan → trial → reflect) with a small group, evaluating the quality of creative thinking applied.

Explore how Indigenous Australian communities pass on physical skills through traditional outdoor activities and collaborative problem-solving — examining what this suggests about how movement knowledge is built and shared.
Compare solutions across groups who solved the same movement challenge differently, analysing what the variety reveals about creative thinking and the constraints each group was working within.

AC9HP4M08.minimum_width: Collaborate to create at least two rules for a physical activity that address fairness or inclusion; apply rules appropriately in at least one physical activity; take on an officiating role and make at least two rule-based decisions.
AC9HP4M08.typical_width: Collaboratively design rule sets across different game types; apply rules fairly with explanation of decisions; officiate in physical activities across multiple rounds; compare fair play principles across game contexts including rules and scoring systems from traditional games of First Nations Australians.
wider: Explore rules and scoring systems used in traditional games of First Nations Australians and compare them to rules and systems used in other games they have played, examining how each system reflects cultural values.
Design and trial a peer officiating feedback process — establishing criteria for good officiating and using them to observe and debrief a peer's officiating performance.

Investigate how rule design differs between inclusive games (e.g. modified sport for disability, community versions of games) and exclusive competitive formats — examining the values embedded in each design.

AC9HP4M09.minimum_width: Use cooperative skills to complete at least one partner or group movement task; maintain possession in a small-sided game by passing and communicating with teammates; propose and implement at least one modification to make a physical activity more inclusive.
AC9HP4M09.typical_width: Apply cooperative skills across varied partner, small group and team movement tasks; use possession-maintenance strategies across game types; modify physical activities in multiple ways (equipment, rules, playing space, number of players) to promote inclusion.
wider: Research how disability sport has adapted mainstream game rules and equipment to enable participation, and apply one adaptive principle to a class activity.
Design a fully modified version of a known game for players with a specific additional need — trialling and refining the design based on peer feedback and the player's experience.
Investigate cooperative skill differences across movement task types (partner balance, team game, performance task) and create a practical guide to cooperative skills for each context.

AC9HP4P01.minimum_width: Explain how at least one person overcame challenge or setback and describe what this meant for their identity or resilience; describe how one physical activity experience (success, challenge or failure) affected their own sense of self.
AC9HP4P01.typical_width: Investigate multiple stories and examples of how success, challenge, setbacks and failure strengthen resilience and identities across different contexts — texts, sport, physical activity, and community examples; discuss how diverse cultural backgrounds shape responses to adversity.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australians' pride in cultural background strengthens identities and resilience — using community stories, athletes or leaders as examples and engaging respectfully with cultural knowledge.
Explore how responses to success, challenge, setbacks and failure are influenced by cultural beliefs and values, comparing examples from at least two different cultural contexts.
Design a personal or class reflective record of physical activity experiences that tracks how experiences of success, challenge and failure influence confidence and identity over a unit.

AC9HP4P02.minimum_width: Identify at least two types of changes people experience as they grow older; identify at least two trusted people or sources for support during puberty or change; practise at least one coping strategy and reflect on its usefulness.
AC9HP4P02.typical_width: Discuss physical, social and emotional changes across multiple transitions including puberty; identify and evaluate a range of support sources; practise and compare coping strategies across different change and challenge scenarios.
wider: Explore the nature of family support networks in First Nations Australian communities and discuss how a wide range of family and community members support young people through changes and transitions.
Analyse text or scenario characters experiencing change and transition — evaluating the effectiveness of their responses and identifying additional or alternative strategies.
Develop a personal coping toolkit documenting strategies that work for them across different types of challenges, with reflection on what each strategy is best suited for.

AC9HP4P03.minimum_width: Identify at least one stereotype in a text or media example and describe the message it sends; describe what unfair treatment based on stereotypes means; propose one way to make a role or responsibility more equitable.
AC9HP4P03.typical_width: Identify and analyse stereotypes in texts and media; discuss how stereotypes lead to unfair treatment and connect to human rights; describe and practise ways to make roles and responsibilities fair, equitable and inclusive across home, school and community contexts.
wider: Design an audit of roles and responsibilities in a familiar context (classroom tasks, household chores, sport roles) to identify where stereotyping is influencing distribution, and propose a fairer system.
Analyse how stereotypes in media targeting children (toys, clothing, advertisements, games) limit choices and reinforce expectations — comparing across two different media contexts or time periods.
Investigate how stereotyped expectations about gender in physical activity limit participation and discuss what schools and communities can do to create more equitable participation cultures.

AC9HP4P04.minimum_width: Predict how another person might feel in a challenging situation and suggest one supportive action; identify and describe at least two strategies for showing respect for diversity; identify at least two forms of bullying and propose one bystander strategy.
AC9HP4P04.typical_width: Apply perspective-taking and empathy across varied challenging scenarios; explore strategies for respecting difference and diversity across personal, school and community contexts; recognise bullying across online and offline contexts and practise bystander and help-seeking strategies.
wider: Explore how demonstrating respect and empathy for First Nations Australians can build positive relationships — investigating specific cultural contexts and what respectful engagement looks like in practice.
Research and participate in games from different cultural heritages, reflecting on how engagement in cultural activities is itself a form of respect and relationship-building.
Investigate the distinction between bystander, upstander and target roles, and practise upstander strategies across both online and offline bullying scenarios.

AC9HP4P05.minimum_width: Identify and describe at least one aspect of a cultural background different from their own; describe at least one connection between valuing diversity and wellbeing; identify at least one safe bystander action for unfair or disrespectful behaviour.
AC9HP4P05.typical_width: Celebrate and explore cultural diversity of the class and community; describe how valuing diversity influences wellbeing through belonging and connection; describe and practise safe bystander actions across different scenarios.
wider: Recognise the important role of cultural narratives in First Nations Australian communities and explore how stories describe diversity and share beliefs and practices.
Explore the diversity of backgrounds, experiences and practices of Asian cultures and connect this to understanding of Australian cultural diversity.
Investigate the concept of 'bystander effect' at an age-appropriate level and discuss how this understanding changes their approach to acting when they witness unfair behaviour.

AC9HP4P06.minimum_width: Identify at least one trigger and one warning sign for a strong emotional response; describe a helpful response during an emergency; practise at least one self-regulation strategy and reflect on its effectiveness.
AC9HP4P06.typical_width: Analyse scenarios to identify triggers, warning signs and emotional responses; discuss helpful responses in emergency contexts with reference to emotional regulation; practise and compare self-regulation strategies across different emotional scenarios.
wider: Explore mindfulness-based self-regulation practices (breathing, body scan, visualisation) and practise one regularly, tracking effectiveness across different emotional situations.
Investigate how athletes and performers use self-regulation strategies under pressure, applying one technique in a physical activity context.
Explore how cultural backgrounds and family norms influence what triggers strong emotions and what counts as an appropriate response — using examples from different cultural contexts.

AC9HP4P07.minimum_width: Practise at least one strategy for seeking consent and one for giving or denying consent; identify at least two actions they can take when something is done without their permission, including at least one online scenario.
AC9HP4P07.typical_width: Rehearse and refine strategies for seeking, giving and denying consent across varied contexts including digital; explore response strategies for unsafe situations both online and offline; describe situations in which permission is required.
wider: Explore how consent applies in digital contexts (photo sharing, tagging, personal information) and practise consent and refusal strategies appropriate for online interactions.
Develop a personal safety plan identifying trusted adults, response strategies and reporting options for different types of unsafe situations, both online and offline.
Analyse increasingly complex consent scenarios and evaluate which response strategies are most appropriate, explaining the reasoning.

AC9HP4P08.minimum_width: Describe at least two warning signs (physical, emotional and/or external) of an unsafe situation; describe a protective behaviour relevant to at least two different contexts; identify at least one help-seeking strategy for a challenging situation.
AC9HP4P08.typical_width: Describe warning signs across all three categories; examine protective behaviours for a full range of situations including water, roads, parks, personal space and online contexts; identify and discuss help-seeking strategies appropriate to different online and offline challenging situations.
wider: Create a personalised safety reference by indicating safe places and trusted people on a local map or area guide, for use in their own neighbourhood.
Design a 'where to go for help' resource for a younger student — identifying trusted adults, reporting pathways and information sources with brief explanations of what each provides.
Practise navigating an online reporting or help-seeking process, building familiarity with digital safety tools and reporting options.

AC9HP4P09.minimum_width: Identify at least two sources of health information and examine one for accuracy; identify a food or nutrition health message and describe the behaviour it promotes; reflect on one health decision influenced by a health message.
AC9HP4P09.typical_width: Access and compare health information from multiple source types (brochures, websites, TV, advertisements, food labels); examine food and nutrition messages from multiple sources; investigate the level of influence different sources have on personal health decisions.
wider: Investigate how advertising and commercial interests bias health information — examining a food or health product advertisement and evaluating whether health claims are supported by evidence.

Audit health messages in a school canteen menu, supermarket display or cereal packaging — identifying what behaviours are promoted, who benefits, and whether messages align with evidence-based advice.
Develop a personal framework for evaluating health information before acting on it — identifying the questions to ask and the criteria to apply.

AC9HP4P10.minimum_width: Identify at least two safe substance storage rules; describe at least one benefit of eating from each main food group; describe what belonging and connection mean and explain their relationship to mental health; identify one behaviour that benefits both health and the environment.
AC9HP4P10.typical_width: Investigate safe storage of medications and substances; explore benefits of eating patterns aligned with the Australian Guide to Healthy Eating; discuss the importance of belonging and connection for mental health and wellbeing; investigate behaviours that support both personal health and environmental sustainability.
wider: Design and implement a small sustainability and health project (e.g. classroom composting, school garden contribution, active transport mapping) and reflect on its health, social and environmental benefits.
Explore how community fruit and vegetable gardens support both health and sustainability — including examples from First Nations food and land practices.
Practise mindfulness and meditation strategies as mental health tools, engaging with at least one technique regularly across a period of time and reflecting on its effects on wellbeing.
